extracted.intended_audience: students of literary history / comparative literature (lecture / study questions)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of guided study/exam questions for lectures on the history of philosophy, religion, and literature (Classical, Oriental, Medieval, and Teutonic). These questions indicate the analytical dimensions students should address when studying authors, movements, languages, transmission, genres, and cultural influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of oriental opinions on Greek thought
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the effect of oriental opinions? — Where can we trace it? — What was the effect of orientalopinions on the growth of infidelity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions ask students to trace Oriental (Indian, Persian, Egyptian, Chinese) influences in Greek thought and literature, citing examples (Sextus Empiricus, Lucian, Plutarch) and historical points such as Julian's reign; examine channels of transmission and measurable intellectual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and aims of the Platonic system
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the great leading principle of Plato? Explain it. — What does Plato regard as the fountain of all knowledge of God? — What does he do in the negative part of his work? — What in the positive? — Is his philosophy complete?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on Plato's epistemology/metaphysics (Forms, source of knowledge), his dialectical method, the balance of negative and positive argumentation, completeness of system, connection to Socrates and later followers, and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's character and philosophical defects
rubrics_metrics.description: What character is given of Aristotle? — What complaint is made of him? — What is the cause of his obscurity? — How does he define virtue? — What are the defects of Aristotle's philosophy? — What is his rank among philosophers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze Aristotle's method (empiricism, teleology), reasons for perceived obscurity, his ethical theory (virtue as mean), cosmology, the senses/experience emphasis and where it succeeds/fails; compare his stature to other philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of Plato and Aristotle
rubrics_metrics.description: Who were the two greatest masters of Grecian philosophy? — Explain their different characteristics. — Which is the model of Greek art? Which of Grecian science?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare and contrast their intellectual temperaments, methods, aims (idealism vs empirical classification), and their respective cultural/disciplinary legacies (Plato: art/ideal; Aristotle: science/system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of mixing Platonic and Aristotelian elements
rubrics_metrics.description: What was compounded out of these two elements? — What is its character? — In what respects is Aristotle great and unrivalled?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify syntheses formed in later thought, their character (practical vs speculative), and which components contributed to enduring strengths in Western philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and influence of Greek vs Oriental philosophies
rubrics_metrics.description: In what did the Greek philosophy differ from the oriental? — What did the Greek writers reverence? — What did they derive from Egypt? — Had they any sympathy with the Hebrews or Persians?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare cosmologies, anthropologies, religious-moral emphases; consider evidence for borrowings/adaptations from Egyptian, Persian, Hebrew thought and their influence on Greek authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and value of Hebrew sacred writings
rubrics_metrics.description: What merit belongs to the sacred writings of the Hebrews? — What is the character of the preceptive part? The historical? — What is the character of the book of Job?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral/preceptive vs historical portions, literary qualities, uniqueness compared to neighboring literatures, and particular features (e.g., Book of Job as exemplifying a certain character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative religions: Hebrews, Persians, Egyptians, Indians
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the doctrine of Moses? — What were some of the features of the Persian religion? — What do the Indian doctrines show? — What resemblances exist between Persians, Scandinavians, Indians, Greeks?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt to compare doctrines (sacrifice, transmigration, eschatology), rites (burials, sacrifices), ethical systems, and to weigh relative antiquity, mutual influences, and points of convergence/divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funerary customs as cultural evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: How did the Greeks dispose of their dead? — How have others disposed of theirs (Egyptian embalming, Zoroastrian/Tibetan practices)? — What is most agreeable to nature? — How are such customs expressive?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use burial/embalming practices to infer beliefs about death, afterlife, and cultural values; compare symbolic meanings and contradictions (e.g., Egyptian embalming vs belief in transmigration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and character of Indian religious/literary doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the most ancient Indian work? — What does it embrace? — How is it composed? — What is said of its maxims and doctrine? — Was this doctrine influential?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss composition, chronology, content (epic/myth/ethical instruction), role of Puranas and possible falsifications, and transmission/canonical status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian poetry: form, moral feeling, and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the character of Indian poetry? — What is its moral feeling? — Which poems are remarkable for joy and the inspiration of love? — What is the character of their translations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine thematic focuses (love, heroism, religion), stylistic traits (descriptive, rhythmic), social practices reflected (widow self-immolation), and quality/faithfulness of translations into English/French.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmigration and its transmission to Greeks
rubrics_metrics.description: On what did the Indian doctrine of transmigration depend? — How did it consist with Platonism? — How did the Greeks obtain knowledge of the doctrine of transmigration?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace intellectual routes for transmission (trade, conquest), philosophical compatibilities/incompatibilities, and historical timing (Alexander, trade links).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade, commerce and routes as vectors of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: What commerce existed? — What is remarked of the African trade? — What proves the ancient connection of Egypt and India? — How did Alexander and his army regard the Hindoos?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commercial links (Egypt-India-Africa-China) and military contacts to explain cultural exchange, evidence in monuments/descriptions, and the role of merchants and armies in diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodization and epochs of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: What three periods of literature has he examined? — What is the principal object in examining authors between Hadrian and Justinian? — What is the duty of historians of literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss criteria for dividing literary history into periods, what each period’s salient features are (invention vs refinement), and methodological cautions for literary historians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and functions of medieval (Latin & vernacular) literature
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the two elements of middle age literature? — What was the object of the Latin Christian literature? Of the vernacular literature? — Who were the first patrons of modern literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze dual streams (learned Latin vs vernacular popular forms), their aims (doctrinal/legal vs national/romantic), patronage structures, and how these shaped content and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of Latin and Lingua Rustica on vernaculars
rubrics_metrics.description: Why was Latin necessary? — What was the effect of Latin on the development of vernacular dialects? — What was the Lingua Rustica? — When did Latin cease to be a living language?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how Latin both preserved knowledge and impeded vernacular growth, accounting for provincialisms, decline of vernacular usage, and later revival/polishing of national tongues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and instances of text loss, falsification and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: What works have been lost? — Were the Puranas falsified? — Were valuable works lost by mere carelessness? — What occasioned losses (collectors, transcribers, wars)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider manuscript transmission problems, deliberate falsification, historical episodes causing loss, and differing standards of textual preservation across ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runic and alphabetic origins in Teutonic inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the Germans probably have an alphabet of their own? — What is said of the Runic alphabet? — How widely are Runic inscriptions diffused? — Where may the Runic alphabet have come from?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess runic evidence for literacy, geographic spread, possible origins (Mediterranean, Baltic), and functions (monuments, magical inscriptions, record-keeping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of Germanic and Romance dialects
rubrics_metrics.description: How does he explain the origin of the High Dutch? — How was it modified in the south? — Which Romanic dialect was first polished? — When did the third polishing take place?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace linguistic mixing (Gothic, Latin, local dialects), regional divergences, stages of standardization/polishing, and literary consequences for national literatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features and varieties of chivalric/romantic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: What machinery was introduced in chivalrous poems? — What is the tone of Arthurian poetry? — What beautifies and ennobles it? — What is Schlegel's beau ideal of a chivalrous poem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine motifs (magic, Graal, knights, adventures), the moral/aesthetic tone, heroic/romantic ideals, and criteria for successful imitation or modern composition in the mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of the Crusades and Oriental fables on European romance
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the nature of the influence of the Crusades? — How did Arabian, Persian, and other Oriental tales reach and affect Europe? — What are the differences between fabliaux and Arabian tales?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cross-cultural borrowing, specific narrative types (Alexander legends, Persian Book of Heroes), and how the Crusades facilitated a chaotic mixture of motifs that shaped medieval romance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard(s) for evaluating romantic/romance fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: By what standard is the merit of romantic fictions measured? — What is the essential mark of distinction between the fictions of Christendom and all others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss evaluative criteria (coherence, moral purpose, imaginative scope, national spirit), and what uniquely Christian elements (aim, symbolism, ethics) differentiate European romances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres: epic, lyric, dramatic — distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: What is remarked of epic poetry? The epic poet? Of dramatic poetry? — Why must we not expect much variety in lyrical poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider formal constraints, thematic range, typical functions of each genre, and historical conditions shaping their development in various periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love-poetry (Provençal, German, Italian, Spanish): traits and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the Gay Science? — Where did the poetry of love flourish? — How was the poetry of love affected by national peculiarities? — What is said of Laura and Petrarch?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare regional traditions of courtly love, formal features (song, troubadour conventions), national inflections, translations, and critical objections to repetition or lack of variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of political events and patrons in literary development
rubrics_metrics.description: What did Charlemagne collect? — For what is Charlemagne entitled to gratitude? — What was the effect of the Mahometan conquests, the Crusades, Danish expeditions, papal power on literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze patronage, courtly culture, political stability/instability, conquest and trade, and institutional influences (church, court) as enabling or constraining literary production.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character, mythology and literary identity
rubrics_metrics.description: With whom do the Persians resemble in religion, poetry, mythology? — Whom do the Indians resemble in mythology and morals? — What national peculiarities distinguish Scandinavian from Greek theology?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative motifs to identify a nation's literary character: mythic archetypes, moral emphases, ceremonial practices, and how these shape literary outputs like heroic sagas and lyric songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the true end of poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open normative prompt: discuss the aims of poetry (education, delight, moral ennoblement, imaginative expression), historic perspectives (classical, medieval, romantic) and how they inform evaluation.
